claim: As on 1 Jan 2016, in posts and services under the Central Government, representation of SCs, STs and OBCs was 17.49%, 8.47% and 21.57% (78 Ministries/Departments reporting). SC and ST were above the prescribed 15% and 7.5%; OBC was below 27%.
source: PIB, Ministry of Personnel (Lok Sabha written reply by Dr Jitendra Singh), 'Representation of Reserved Categories', 17 Jul 2019
note: Same release: OBC share was 16.55% on 1.1.2012 and rose as the OBC quota (begun Sept 1993) matured. Stock figure, not a flow figure.

claim: Same release: ten Ministries/Departments (with over 90% of central employees, incl. PSBs and CPSUs) had 92,589 backlog reserved vacancies (SC 29,198; ST 22,829; OBC 40,562); 63,876 were filled from 1 Apr 2012 to 31 Dec 2016 and 28,713 (SC 8,223; ST 6,955; OBC 13,535) stayed unfilled on 1 Jan 2017.
value: 28,713 unfilled of 92,589 (about 31%, our arithmetic)
source: PIB, Ministry of Personnel (Lok Sabha written reply), 17 Jul 2019; and PIB, Ministry of Social Justice (Lok Sabha written reply), 3 Aug 2021
page_or_section: 2019 release: para 4 (92,589 / 63,876 / 28,713 and splits); 2021 release: table column "As on 31.12.2016" only (8,223 / 6,955 / 13,535)
note: The 2021 reply gives the 28,713 split identically. 31% = 28,713 / 92,589 (our arithmetic). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Corrected: the 2021 reply gives only the 28,713 split by category; 92,589 and 63,876 are in the 2019 release only.

value: backlog did not fall between 2016 and 2019 snapshots (SC 8,223 to 14,366)
source: PIB, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (MoS A. Narayanaswamy, Lok Sabha written reply), 3 Aug 2021
note: Column order read from the repeated header 'As on 31.12.2016 ... 31.12.2019' then SC ST OBC. The release notes DoPT's OM of 16.12.2014 asked every Ministry to set up an in-house committee to find root causes.

claim: DoPT year-ender (17 Jan 2025): over 4 lakh backlog reserved vacancies for SCs, STs and OBCs were filled in 2016-2023, against 1.08 lakh in 2004-2013; SC and ST representation in Central Government services met the prescribed 15% and 7.5% as on 1 Jan 2024; OBC representation in direct recruitment stayed above 27% over the past decade.
value: backlog filled 4 lakh+ (2016-23) v 1.08 lakh (2004-13); SC 15%, ST 7.5% met at 1.1.2024
source: PIB, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, 'Year Ender 2024: DoPT', 17 Jan 2025
note: Government's own summary; gives no group-wise (A/B/C/D) split or exact percentages. Group A and top-grade shares were not found in a primary release (see NOTES).

claim: DoPT OM No. 36033/1/2013-Estt.(Res.) of 13 Sep 2017 raised the creamy-layer income criterion for OBCs from Rs 6 lakh to Rs 8 lakh a year, effective 1 Sep 2017. Earlier steps: Rs 1 lakh (OM of 8 Sep 1993), 2.5 lakh (9 Mar 2004), 4.5 lakh (14 Oct 2008), 6 lakh (27 May 2013).
value: Rs 8 lakh gross annual (parental) income
source: DoPT Office Memorandum, 13 Sep 2017, as hosted by the National Commission for Backward Classes
second_source: PIB, Ministry of Social Justice (Rajya Sabha written reply by Dr Virendra Kumar), 9 Feb 2022
note: The 2022 reply says the Rs 8 lakh parental-income limit stood on 9 Feb 2022. Whether it has been raised since 9 Feb 2022 was not checked; a search surfaced a 2024-25 parliamentary committee report (eparlib) saying no proposal was pending, but that report could not be opened (BLOCKED), so do not state 'unchanged since 2017' as fact.

claim: There is no creamy-layer exclusion for SC and ST reservation in the executive policy: the Minister said (5 Feb 2020) 'there is no concept of creamy layer' for SC/ST. For OBCs an Expert Committee under B.P. Sharma (former DoPT Secretary), set up on 8 Mar 2019 to study creamy-layer equivalence, reported on 17 Sep 2019 and was under consideration.
value: no creamy layer for SC/ST in policy (Feb 2020)
source: PIB, Ministry of Social Justice (MoS Krishan Pal Gurjar, Rajya Sabha written reply), 5 Feb 2020
note: Position of the Government in 2020. The Supreme Court's 2024 opinions on whether the creamy-layer idea can reach SC/ST are in claims -08 to -11, -13 and ledger POL03-C16.

claim: Rohini Commission (sub-categorisation of OBCs): appointed by notification dated 2 Oct 2017 with Justice G. Rohini (retd Chief Justice, Delhi High Court) as chair; it was to examine the uneven distribution of reservation benefits among OBCs and work out criteria for sub-categorisation. It submitted its report to the President on 31 Jul 2023.
value: report submitted 31 Jul 2023
source: PIB, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, 'OBC Sub-Categorisation Report Delivered to President', 31 Jul 2023
note: The release gives no findings. CONFLICT on date: para 49 of the Davinder Singh judgment says the Rohini Commission was set up 'in 2007' (official copy, PDF p.27); PIB says 2 Oct 2017. Use PIB. The report's recommendations were not found in any primary publication. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Removed "under Article 340": the PIB release does not say it. CONFLICT source corrected: the "in 2007" wording is Mithal J.'s opinion, para 49, PDF p.537 (not para 49 of the CJI opinion, not PDF p.27).

claim: Davinder Singh, opinion of Chandrachud CJI (for himself and Manoj Misra J.), conclusion (e)-(f), para 205: SCs are 'a socially heterogenous class'; a State may sub-classify SCs under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) if there is a rational principle with a nexus to the purpose; Chinnaiah's bar on sub-classification is overruled.
value: Chinnaiah overruled; sub-classification of SCs allowed on rational principle + nexus
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Ledger POL03-C15 gives the 6:1 split and Art 14/15(4)/16(4) holding. This row adds the quoted conclusion.

claim: Davinder Singh, para 205(f)(i)-(ii): the State may sub-classify 'based on inadequate representation of certain castes' but must show the inadequacy is because of backwardness; it must collect data on inadequacy of representation in State services, used as an indicator of backwardness.
value: State must collect data on representation in services
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Answers 'way forward': the Court itself ties sub-classification to data.

claim: Davinder Singh, para 205(f)(iii): Article 335 (efficiency of administration) is not a limitation on the power under Articles 16(1) and 16(4) but a restatement of the need to consider SC/ST claims; efficiency must be viewed in a way that promotes inclusion.
value: Art 335 not a limit on Arts 16(1)/16(4)
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Relevant if an examiner expects 'efficiency' as a reason benefits do not reach the SC/ST.

claim: Davinder Singh, CJI opinion: sub-classification differs from the creamy layer because (i) economic advancement does not offset the social discrimination faced by SCs, (ii) creamy layer excludes the socially advanced while sub-classification identifies those facing most discrimination, (iii) sub-classification is qualitative inclusion v exclusion, (iv) preference identifies castes in the list while creamy layer applies to individuals.
value: four distinctions, items (i)-(iv)
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: CJI opinion, summary item 'g' (printed Part B, PDF p.20 area)
note: Item letter 'g' is inside the opinion's own summary of its reasoning; the PDF page was located from the text layer (page 20).

claim: Punjab Scheduled Castes and Backward Classes (Reservation in Services) Act, 2006: s.4(2) reserves 25% of direct-recruitment vacancies for SCs and 12% for Backward Classes; s.4(5) offers half of the SC quota to Balmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs 'as a first preference'. The Punjab and Haryana High Court struck s.4(5) down on 29 Mar 2010 (following Chinnaiah).
value: 25% SC; 50% of it first preference to two castes
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: The Act's short title is read from the judgment's footnote 'Punjab Act' (PDF p.7); the year 2006 appears there. The Supreme Court 2024 ruling upheld the principle; it did not decide each Punjab clause (the matters were sent to a regular Bench, para 206). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: the Act and its title are in para 6 on p.7; ss.4(2), 4(5) and the 29 Mar 2010 High Court judgment on p.8. Section 4(5) says "if available" (Balmikis and Mazhabi Sikhs).

claim: Davinder Singh, Trivedi J. (dissent), paras 67-70: records that concurring opinions in E.V. Chinnaiah (Sema J., Sinha J.) and the five-judge Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) held the creamy-layer principle not applicable to SC/ST, who are separate classes under the Presidential List. Gavai J. (para 295, ledger POL03-C16) and Vikram Nath, Mithal and Sharma JJ. favoured excluding the creamy layer.
value: Court's opinions split on creamy layer for SC/ST; no binding holding in the order
source: State of Punjab v Davinder Singh, judgment 1 Aug 2024 (seven judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Trivedi J. dissent paras 67-70, PDF pp.495-497; ledger C16 for the other opinions
note: Neutral summary: the Court's order (para 205, ledger C15) did not decide creamy layer for SC/ST; the ledger lists where each judge stands. Page range 495-497 located from the text layer (para 67 on PDF p.495).

claim: Higher education, AISHE 2021-22: enrolment SC 66.23 lakh, ST 27.1 lakh, OBC 1.63 crore, total 4.33 crore. Gross Enrolment Ratio: all 28.4, SC 25.9, ST 21.2.
value: SC 15.3% / ST 6.3% / OBC 37.6% of enrolment (our arithmetic); GER SC 25.9, ST 21.2 v all 28.4
source: PIB, Ministry of Education, 'AISHE 2021-22', 25 Jan 2024
note: Shares computed by us: 66.23/433, 27.1/433 (lakh/crore converted), 163/433. The AISHE final-report tables themselves were not read; the figures are the Ministry's press summary.

claim: Higher education, AISHE 2023-24: enrolment SC 69.72 lakh, ST 28.83 lakh, OBC 1.80 crore; GER SC 27.8, ST 22.8 against 30 overall (23.7 in 2014-15). Total enrolment 4.5 crore.
value: SC 15.5% / ST 6.4% / OBC 40.0% of 4.5 crore (our arithmetic); GER gap ST 22.8 v 30
source: PIB, Ministry of Education, release on AISHE 2022-23 and 2023-24 reports, 8 Jul 2026; total enrolment from Lok Sabha Unstarred Q.143, 20 Jul 2026

source: PIB, Ministry of Education (MoS Sukanta Majumdar, Lok Sabha written reply), 3 Aug 2026

claim: Group-wise representation in Central Government posts as on 1 Jan 2024 (data from 80 Ministries/Departments; total 32,52,152 employees): Group A 1,19,178 employees: SC 14.20%, ST 6.54%, OBC 19.14%. Group B 3,64,307: SC 16.20%, ST 7.63%, OBC 21.95%. Group C excluding Safai Karamchari 27,27,930: SC 16.75%, ST 8.94%, OBC 27.29%. Safai Karamchari (Group C) 40,737: SC 36.75%, ST 8.18%, OBC 21.15%. All: SC 16.84%, ST 8.70%, OBC 26.32%.
source: DoPT Annual Report 2024-25 (Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions), Chapter 4, para 4.8
note: Read 2026-11-10 in the DoPT Annual Report 2024-25 (file listed on dopt.gov.in's document store, report dated 17 Dec 2024). Quotas to compare: 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC in direct recruitment (same report, para 4.3). Reading: SC and ST are below quota in Group A (14.20 v 15; 6.54 v 7.5) and OBC well below 27 (19.14); quotas are met only in lower groups; sanitation work is where SC representation is 36.75%. The comparisons are ours; the report itself says nothing about 'concentration'. Media outlets quote the same table. Replaces the earlier 'no table found' note; NOTES line on group-wise data is now closed.

claim: The DoPT Annual Report states the reservation rules: in direct recruitment on all-India open competition 15% SC, 7.5% ST, 27% OBC; otherwise than by open competition 16.66%, 7.5% and 25.84%; in promotion only SC and ST (15% and 7.5%); the OBC creamy-layer income limit was 'presently Rs.8.0 lakh per annum'; total reservation must not exceed the 50% limit set by the nine-judge Indira Sawhney bench; promotion OMs of 13 Aug 1997 and 10 Aug 2010 are sub judice (Jarnail Singh, 28 Jan 2022; DoPT OM of 12 Apr 2022 asks for quantifiable data on inadequacy of representation).
value: 15/7.5/27 quotas; promotion SC/ST only; 50% cap; Rs 8 lakh
source: DoPT Annual Report 2024-25 (Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions), Chapter 4, para 4.8
note: Read 2026-11-10. The report spells the case 'Indira Sawhney'. The Rs 8 lakh limit matches claim -05 as of the report date; whether it has changed since was not checked.

claim: Lok Sabha, 3 Dec 2025 (DoPT): 'over 4.80 lakh backlog vacancies have been filled up since 2016'. The Government's measures: an In-House Committee in every Ministry/Department to identify backlog reserved vacancies and the root cause; Special Recruitment Drives; a Liaison Officer of Deputy Secretary rank or above and a Special Reservation Cell. The reply gives no group-wise (A, B, C, D) or Ministry-wise split of unfilled posts, though the question asked for it.
value: >4.80 lakh backlog vacancies filled since 2016; no unfilled count given
source: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 687, 'Unfilled Posts Reserved for SC/ST/OBC', answered 3 Dec 2025, Department of Personnel and Training (Dr Jitendra Singh)
note: Read at sansad.in 2026-11-10. This updates claim -04 ('over 4 lakh, 2016-2023'). The question's own part (a) asked for unfilled posts group-wise and the Government answered without numbers: do not state the current backlog size. The 2019-era backlog tables are claim -03.

claim: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 1384 (31 Jul 2024, DoPT): asked for total OBC vacancies in the Central Government as on 31 May 2024; the answer gave the quotas (15/7.5/27; promotion for SC and ST up to the lowest rung of Group A) and said 'The data regarding vacancies is maintained by respective Ministries/Departments', with no total.
value: no consolidated vacancy figure given by DoPT (2024)
source: Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 1384, 'Vacancies of Reserved Category', 31 Jul 2024, Department of Personnel and Training
